tagline: The impulse approximation rescues energy
question_text: Why does kinetic energy vanish in a collision but momentum does not?
audio_script: Watch two carts collide head-on. Momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy is not. Before the collision the two carts carry a certain kinetic energy. After the collision, that energy is smaller. Where did it go? Into heat, into sound, into the deformation of the carts. The trick is that momentum is a vector and Newton's third law guarantees the two carts receive equal and opposite impulses. Energy is a scalar, and it can change form. This is why momentum conservation is robust while energy conservation is delicate. Ohanian's guide adds a subtle point. The reason momentum is conserved during a collision is not that external forces are absent. It is that they are small compared to the collision forces and they act over an extremely short window. So their impulse is negligible. This is the impulse approximation. Friction, gravity, air resistance — they all push on the carts, but during the one millisecond of contact, they deliver almost nothing. Momentum is effectively frozen for that millisecond. After the collision, friction takes over and slowly bleeds the motion away. But by then the collision is already over. The approximation separates the fast event from the slow event. That is why the equations work, and why they fail when you try to apply them to a slow collision — say a spring being compressed gently. There, the collision time is long, external forces get a chance to act, and momentum is no longer conserved. Fast events hide the world. Slow events reveal it.

header_title: A Wave Is Not the Medium
tagline: The pattern travels while the particles stay put
question_text: Does the medium move with the wave?
audio_script: Pluck a guitar string. A wave travels from one end to the other. Now watch a single point on the string. It moves up and down. It does not travel with the wave. This is one of the most confusing ideas in wave physics. The wave is the pattern. The medium oscillates in place. When the wave arrives at a point, the point rises, falls, rises again. When the wave leaves, the point is back where it started. Nothing has moved except the disturbance. Ohanian's study guide stresses this distinction with the term worldline. A worldline is the path of a single point through space and time. For a wave on a string, the worldlines of individual points are vertical oscillations. The wave pattern is a diagonal envelope cutting across them. The speed of the wave is not the speed of any particle. It is the speed of the pattern. On a string, that speed is the square root of tension divided by linear density. Tighten the string, wave speeds up. Make it heavier, wave slows down. This is why thick bass strings play low notes on a guitar. Slower wave, longer wavelength, lower pitch. The pattern is the message. The medium is just the messenger.

tagline: When the fluid cannot get underneath
question_text: When does the buoyant force disappear?
audio_script: Archimedes' principle says an immersed body feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid. Textbook. Now picture a block sealed with wax to the bottom of a tank. Water flows over it, around it, but not under it. What does the block feel? Only downward pressure from above. No upward pressure from below, because there is no fluid below. The block is held down. Archimedes' principle fails. This is not a paradox. It is a warning about the assumptions hiding inside every formula. Archimedes assumes the fluid forms a continuous layer under the body. When that layer is broken, the upward pressure force vanishes. A suction cup works the same way. A ship that runs aground and seals against the mud can be stuck, even though it floats perfectly well in open water. The math of buoyancy is correct only when the fluid reaches all around the object. Break the continuity, and you break the buoyancy. Ohanian's study guide uses this example to make a broader point. Physics formulas are maps of a specific terrain. When you walk off the map, the formula does not bend. It just stops applying. The careful student asks not only what the formula says but what it assumes.

header_title: Why You Are Safe Inside a Conductor
tagline: The electric field cannot penetrate
question_text: Why is the field inside a conductor zero?
audio_script: Put a metal sphere in a strong electric field. What happens inside the metal? Nothing. The field is zero. Here is why. The conduction electrons inside the metal are free to move. If there were an electric field inside, they would feel a force and they would move. But they cannot move in a steady state, because that would be a current, and by assumption nothing is happening. So the charges rearrange themselves on the surface until they cancel the external field exactly at every interior point. The field inside is zero. Every bit of net charge ends up on the surface. This single result, which falls straight out of Gauss's law, explains a lot. It is why a car protects you from lightning. The current travels on the outer skin and never reaches you. It is why a Faraday cage shields sensitive electronics. It is why a charged conductor has all of its charge on the surface no matter how you try to distribute it inside. And it is why a sharp point on a conductor has a much stronger field than a smooth surface does. The charge crowds at the tip. This last fact is why lightning rods work. Pointy metal up high. The field is strongest there. The lightning strikes the rod instead of the roof.

tagline: Lenz's law is energy conservation in disguise
question_text: Why does an induced current always oppose its cause?
audio_script: Move a magnet toward a coil. A current flows. Now pull the magnet away. A current flows the other way. In both cases the current opposes the change. Push the magnet in, and the induced current creates a field that pushes back. Pull the magnet out, and the induced current creates a field that pulls in. This is Lenz's law. It is often presented as a rule to memorize — the minus sign in Faraday's equation. But it is actually a consequence of energy conservation. Suppose the opposite. Suppose the current went the other way. Then when you push the magnet in, the induced current would pull the magnet in faster, which would induce more current, which would pull harder, and the system would run away. You would get energy from nothing. Lenz's law says no. The universe resists change. Move a metal plate through a magnetic field, and eddy currents form inside it that resist the motion. This is magnetic braking, used in high-speed trains and roller coasters. Move a superconductor through a magnetic field, and the currents become perfect, and the material can float on a magnet. Lenz's law is not a rule of thumb. It is energy conservation wearing a magnetic disguise.

tagline: Photons carry momentum
question_text: How does sunlight exert force?
audio_script: Light carries energy. Does it also carry momentum? Yes. Every photon has momentum equal to its energy divided by c. Shine a laser on a mirror, and the mirror is pushed. This is radiation pressure, and it is not a curiosity. It is a real, measurable force. Sunlight at Earth's orbit delivers about one thousand three hundred fifty watts per square meter. The radiation pressure from that flux is about four point five microPascals. That is a tiny force. But the Earth intercepts a disk of radius six thousand four hundred kilometers, and the total outward force on the Earth is about five hundred eighty million newtons. That is small compared to the Sun's gravity, which is three point six times ten to the twenty second newtons. So the Earth stays in orbit. But for a solar sail, the pressure is enough. A large, thin, reflective sheet can be accelerated by sunlight with no fuel. Engineers plan to use this to send probes to the outer solar system. The pressure is small but constant. Over years, it adds up. Light pushes, gently but endlessly. This is also why comet tails always point away from the Sun. It is not the solar wind. It is radiation pressure.

header_title: Why Sign Conventions Make You Cry
tagline: The mirror and lens code explained
question_text: Why do mirrors and lenses use opposite sign rules?
audio_script: Ask a physics student what they hate most about optics. The answer is usually sign conventions. For mirrors, focal length is positive if concave, negative if convex. For lenses it is positive if convex, negative if concave. Object and image distances follow different rules. Why? Because mirrors and lenses use the same equation to describe different physical systems. The mirror equation is one over s plus one over s prime equals one over f, where s is in front of the mirror and s prime is in front for a real image. For a lens, s prime is on the opposite side for a real image. The math is the same. The geometry is flipped. The textbook convention handles this by assigning different signs. But here is the trick. Do not memorize the table. Draw a ray diagram first. Trace the light. Where the rays actually converge is the real image. Where they appear to come from is the virtual image. The signs follow the diagram, not the other way around. Students who memorize the table make sign errors. Students who draw the diagram do not. The sign convention is a bookkeeping tool. The picture is the physics.

tagline: Thin film interference in one idea
question_text: What makes the colors on a soap bubble?
audio_script: A soap bubble is a very thin layer of water sandwiched between two layers of air. Sunlight hits it. Some light reflects off the outer surface. Some light passes through the water and reflects off the inner surface. The two reflected rays then travel to your eye, and they can interfere. When they are in phase, you see a bright color. When they are out of phase, that color is missing. What determines the phase? Two things. The extra distance the inner ray travels is twice the thickness of the film. And a phase flip happens when light reflects off a boundary where the index of refraction increases. For a soap bubble in air, the outer reflection flips. The inner one does not. So the interference condition is not what you would guess without thinking. Ohanian's study guide is careful about this. The condition for constructive interference is different from the naive formula because of that one phase flip. This is why bubbles show colors that shift as you watch them. The film thins under gravity. The path difference changes. The color changes. Two rays, one extra path, one phase flip. That is all there is.

tagline: Diffraction limits every telescope
question_text: Why is there a limit to how sharp a telescope can see?
audio_script: Point a telescope at a distant star. It should look like a single bright dot. It does not. It looks like a small disk with faint rings around it. Where does the disk come from? Diffraction. When light passes through a circular opening, the aperture of the telescope, it spreads out. The spread depends on the wavelength and on the diameter of the opening. Bigger opening, tighter spread. Shorter wavelength, tighter spread. But you can never make it zero. For a telescope with a twelve centimeter lens and visible light at five hundred nanometers, the minimum angular separation you can resolve is about one arcsecond. That is why Mount Palomar has a five meter mirror. It is why Hubble has a two and a half meter mirror. Size buys resolution. And it is why radio telescopes, which use much longer wavelengths, must be enormous — hundreds of meters across — to see the same detail that a small optical telescope can. Rayleigh put a number on it. The number rules every telescope ever built. It is the same physics that limits the human eye. Your pupil is about five millimeters, and two car headlights a kilometer away are two bright blobs, not two points.

tagline: Nuclear binding energy and E=mc squared
question_text: Why does a nucleus weigh less than its parts?
audio_script: Take a carbon nucleus. Six protons, six neutrons, six electrons. Weigh the pieces separately. Add them up. Now weigh the whole nucleus. It weighs less. Where did the mass go? It became energy. When the nucleus formed, the protons and neutrons pulled together and released energy. That energy left the nucleus as photons and neutrinos. By special relativity, energy has mass. The energy released had a mass equivalent, and it carried that mass away with it. The nucleus that remains weighs less than the sum of its parts. The difference is called the mass defect. For most nuclei, it is about eight mega-electron-volts per nucleon. That is roughly one percent of the rest-mass energy of the nucleons themselves. It sounds small. It is the entire basis of nuclear power. Four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium nucleus, and the helium weighs less. The difference is the energy that powers the Sun. A uranium nucleus splits, and the fragments weigh less. That difference is the energy of a nuclear reactor. This is the exchange rate between mass and energy, and it is the same everywhere in the universe. Every time you liberate energy, some mass disappears. Every time you bind something, mass appears.

tagline: Differentiate the position vector
question_text: A particle has position r(t) = (6+t)x - 4t^2 y + (8t - 4t^2)z. Find velocity and acceleration.
audio_script: A particle's position is given by r of t equals open paren six plus t close paren x, minus four t squared y, plus open paren eight t minus four t squared close paren z. Find velocity. Differentiate each component. Velocity is one x, minus eight t y, plus open paren eight minus eight t close paren z. Find acceleration. Differentiate again. Acceleration is negative eight y minus eight z. Notice something. The acceleration is constant. It does not depend on time. This happens whenever the position has no powers of t higher than two. If the position has no powers of t higher than one, the velocity is constant. If it has no powers higher than two, the acceleration is constant. This is a useful shortcut. It tells you immediately what kind of motion you are dealing with. Answer A.

tagline: Static equilibrium at the corners
question_text: A 40 cm wide drawer is pulled from one side. Coefficient of friction is 0.60. Maximum offset from centerline?
audio_script: A drawer is forty centimeters wide and twenty centimeters deep. Coefficient of friction is zero point six zero. If you pull only on one side, the drawer tilts and jams. How far from the centerline can you pull without jamming? The answer comes from static equilibrium. The torque from the pulling force must balance the torque from the contact forces at the two front corners. Working it out, x equals half the depth divided by the coefficient of friction. Depth is twenty centimeters. Half is ten. Divide by zero point six zero. That is sixteen point seven. Rounded, seventeen centimeters. Answer C. This is why wide drawers have handles near the center. And why a stuck drawer sometimes opens when you pull from the middle instead of the edge.

tagline: Doppler shift with a moving source
question_text: A train whistle sounds at 440 Hz. The engineer hears the reflected sound at 466 Hz. Train speed?
audio_script: A train whistle at four hundred forty hertz. Sound reflects off a canyon wall. The engineer hears the direct sound and the echo together, and they produce a beat pattern equivalent to a minor second, the ratio four sixty six over four forty. Find the train speed. The reflected sound comes from a source moving toward the wall. Doppler shift, moving source. Then the wall reflects the sound as a stationary source, and the engineer is moving toward it. Combine the two shifts. The frequency ratio is one plus v over c, all squared. Set that equal to four sixty six over four forty. Solve for v. Velocity of sound is about three hundred thirty two meters per second. v comes out to about ten meters per second, or thirty six kilometers per hour. Answer B. This is why a passing train's whistle drops in pitch as it goes by.

tagline: RMS speed and molecular mass
question_text: H2 at 30 Celsius has a certain RMS speed. At what T does O2 have the same RMS speed?
audio_script: Hydrogen gas at thirty degrees Celsius has a certain rms speed. At what temperature would oxygen have the same rms speed? RMS speed is proportional to the square root of T over m. Set them equal. T_H over m_H equals T_O over m_O. Hydrogen is two grams per mole. Oxygen is thirty two grams per mole. Ratio is sixteen. So the temperature of oxygen must be sixteen times the temperature of hydrogen. Careful with scales. T_H is three hundred three kelvin. Multiply by sixteen. That is four thousand eight hundred forty eight kelvin. Answer C, about four thousand eight hundred kelvin. That is a very high temperature. Oxygen molecules are sixteen times heavier than hydrogen, so to move at the same rms speed they need sixteen times the absolute temperature. This is why hydrogen escapes from the Earth's atmosphere. It is light enough to reach escape speed at ordinary temperatures.

tagline: Mechanical equivalent of heat
question_text: Crank a freezer at 2 rev/s with 8 J per rev for 1 hour. Temperature rise of 1 gallon of water?
audio_script: You need to heat a gallon of water. You have an ice cream freezer with an insulated inner container. Crank at two revolutions per second. Each revolution takes eight joules of work. That gives sixteen watts of power. Run for one hour. Total work is sixteen times thirty six hundred, which is fifty seven thousand six hundred joules. Convert to calories. Divide by four point one eight five. That is thirteen thousand eight hundred calories, or thirteen point eight kilocalories. A gallon of water has a mass of three point eight one kilograms. Specific heat of water is one kilocalorie per kilogram per Celsius. Temperature rise is thirteen point eight divided by three point eight one. That is three point six degrees Celsius. Answer B. This is the classic experiment of Joule, updated. Mechanical work becomes heat. The exchange rate is called the mechanical equivalent of heat.

tagline: Coulomb force dwarfs gravity
question_text: What is the ratio of the electric to gravitational force between an electron and a proton?
audio_script: Take an electron and a proton at any distance. Compare the electric force between them to the gravitational force. Both forces follow inverse square laws, so the ratio is independent of distance. Electric force is k e squared over r squared. Gravitational force is G m_e m_p over r squared. Divide. The r squared cancels. Plug in the numbers. k is nine times ten to the ninth. e squared is about two point five six times ten to the negative thirty eight. G is six point six seven times ten to the negative eleven. m_e is nine point one times ten to the negative thirty one. m_p is one point six seven times ten to the negative twenty seven. The ratio comes out to about two point three times ten to the thirty nine. Answer C. Electric force is two thousand billion billion billion billion times stronger. And yet gravity runs the universe, because positive and negative charges cancel each other out on large scales. Mass does not cancel.

tagline: Energy unit for the atomic scale
question_text: A proton falls through a 4500 V potential difference. Gain in kinetic energy?
audio_script: A proton falls through a four thousand five hundred volt potential difference. What kinetic energy does it gain? One electron volt is the energy gained by a charge of e when it falls through one volt. The proton has charge plus e. So it gains four thousand five hundred electron volts. Answer A. In joules, that is four thousand five hundred times one point six times ten to the negative nineteen, which is seven point two times ten to the negative sixteen joules. But for atomic physics, the electron volt is the natural unit. It is the energy scale of atoms, of photons, of chemical bonds. Learn to think in eV. It will save you from carrying around powers of ten all day. One eV is about the energy of a visible photon. Thirteen point six eV is the binding energy of the hydrogen electron. Five hundred thousand eV is the rest energy of an electron. Learn the landmarks and the units stop feeling strange.

header_title: Energy Stored in a Charged Sphere
tagline: Isolated conductor energy
question_text: A sphere of radius 0.20 m carries 1e-7 C. Energy stored?
audio_script: A conducting sphere of radius zero point two meters carries a charge of one times ten to the negative seven coulombs. How much electrical energy is stored? For an isolated conductor, the energy is one half Q V. The potential at the surface is k Q over R. k is nine times ten to the ninth. Q is one times ten to the negative seven. R is zero point two. So V is four thousand five hundred volts. Energy is half of one times ten to the negative seven times four thousand five hundred, which is two point two five times ten to the negative four joules. Answer B. This is the energy you would have to spend to assemble the charge, bringing each bit in from infinity against the repulsion of the bits already there. It is also the energy that would be released if the charge were allowed to fly apart. This is how we estimate the energy stored in a Van de Graaff generator, or in a thundercloud.

tagline: Drift velocity in a copper bar
question_text: A copper bar of cross-section 0.5 cm squared carries 98 A. Drift velocity of electrons?
audio_script: A copper bar with cross section zero point five square centimeters carries ninety eight amperes of current. How fast do the electrons drift? Current equals n e A v_d. Rearrange. v_d equals I over n e A. n for copper is about eight point five times ten to the twenty eight electrons per cubic meter. e is one point six times ten to the negative nineteen. A is zero point five square centimeters, which is five times ten to the negative five meters squared. I is ninety eight. Plug in. v_d is about one point four times ten to the negative four meters per second. Answer A. That is zero point one four millimeters per second. The electrons are drifting slower than a snail. Yet the light comes on instantly, because the electric field propagates through the wire at nearly the speed of light and pushes all the electrons along at once. The signal is fast. The carriers are slow.

header_title: Cosmic Rays in a Magnetic Field
tagline: Radius of curvature in a magnetic field
question_text: A 500 keV proton moves in a magnetic field of period 4.7 s. Find B.
audio_script: A cosmic ray proton completes one circle in a magnetic field every four point seven seconds. The proton has a kinetic energy of five hundred keV. Find the magnetic field. The period is two pi m over q B. So B equals two pi m over q T. m for a proton is one point six seven times ten to the negative twenty seven. q is one point six times ten to the negative nineteen. T is four point seven. Plug in. B comes out to about one point four times ten to the negative eight tesla. Answer B. Compare that to the Earth's magnetic field at the surface, which is about five times ten to the negative five tesla. So the cosmic ray is in an extremely weak field. That is why it takes seconds per orbit. In the galaxy's magnetic field, protons orbit much faster. And in a laboratory cyclotron, the field is around one tesla, and the period is nanoseconds.
